column1: What is the master invariant governing all actuated sorting mechanisms?
column2: The relationship between decision latency (gate actuation time) and object transit time — if gate deflection time exceeds the interval between incoming objects, correct sorting is structurally impossible regardless of control logic quality.

column1: Why does density-based separation fail for sorting LEGO elements?
column2: All standard LEGO elements are molded from ABS plastic with nearly uniform density (~1.05 g/cm³), so there is no meaningful density differential to exploit; sorting must rely on geometric discrimination or optical/capacitive sensing instead.

column1: What is the primary discriminating physical property used in mechanical LEGO sorting hierarchies?
column2: Maximum envelope dimension — the largest measurement of a part that determines whether it can pass through a given aperture, screen, or slot.

column1: What is the coefficient of friction range for ABS plastic (LEGO) against itself, and why does it matter?
column2: Approximately 0.4 to 0.6, depending on surface finish and environment; it governs how parts slide in chutes, tumble in drums, and stack, directly affecting passive sorting mechanism design.

column1: In Lego Technic actuated sorters, what component provides overload protection in a gate's drive train, and what is its function?
column2: The clutch gear (part 76244 or 18947); it defines the maximum torque the system will tolerate, slipping under excess load rather than stripping gears or stalling the motor into thermal shutdown.

column1: What is the 'load balance' invariant in multi-output actuated sorting systems?
column2: Downstream capacity of each output channel must match the fraction of objects it receives; unbalanced channels cause backpressure, jamming, or overflow that cascades upstream and corrupts the sort sequence.

column1: What is the core invariant of sensor-feedback sorting logic, and why does it matter for timing?
column2: Measurement before commitment — classification must complete while the object remains within the sensor's detection zone; at ~5 cm/s belt speed with a 1-2 cm sensor zone, this gives roughly 200-400 ms to read, classify, and dispatch a gate signal.

column1: What does a LEGO Color Sensor actually output, and how is a color label derived?
column2: It outputs reflected light intensity across red, green, blue (and ambient) channels; firmware derives a color label via a threshold-based lookup table calibrated under factory lighting conditions, not an absolute colorimetric value.

column1: What does 'classification confidence, not classification certainty' mean in sensor-based sorting design?
column2: Sorting logic must include a validity check on sensor readings (e.g., is the signal strong/clear enough to trust) before committing to a sort destination, since ambient light, dust, or scratches can shift readings toward incorrect threshold boundaries.

column1: Why does multi-criteria sorting (e.g., color AND size) introduce 'state' into an otherwise stateless sorting system?
column2: Because each criterion may be measured at a different station/time (e.g., color at station one, size at station two), the first reading must persist in memory until the second is complete, and the two readings must be correctly associated with the same object.

column1: What are the approximate dimensions illustrating the 'dimensional hierarchy' invariant between a 2x4 brick and a 1x1 plate?
column2: A 2x4 brick: ~15.8mm width x 31.8mm length x ~17.6mm height (with studs). A 1x1 plate: ~7.8mm x 7.8mm x 3.2mm height — an order-of-magnitude volumetric difference that creates natural sorting boundaries via apertures.

column1: In the mechanical sorting lab, what physical mechanism allows gravity-assisted comparison between tokens representing values 1-8?
column2: Tokens built from 2x2 bricks with stacked 1x1 round plates of varying heights encode integer values; ramp-based height gauges use gravity to mechanically compare token heights, providing both functional comparison and visual confirmation of sort order.
